catalog_quote: In ancient Greek, the pitch accent of most words depends on the syllabification assigned to underlying representations ... Recessive accent. The unmarked accent pattern of Greek words is RECESSIVE ACCENT. The recessively accented syllable is determined as follows: (2) RECESSIVE ACCENT: The accent falls on the penult if the final syllable is heavy, otherwise on the antepenult. ... To apply (2) correctly it is necessary to know that word-final consonants are weightless (extrametrical) in Greek phonology. Therefore, in word-final position, both -V and -VC rhymes make light syllables, whereas -VCC is heavy, as are -VV and -VVC. ... Recessive accent is mandatory for finite verbs and for certain morphological classes of nominals (such as most types of neuter nouns). No word can have the accent further to the left than the recessive accent, but in many words it is further to the right, either …
sweep_summary: The single sweep item for anci1242 (Mangold 2005, Duden Aussprachewörterbuch) is a German pronunciation dictionary that Glottolog's own record marks as a computerized misassignment to Ancient Greek from the word 'ausführliche'; it is irrelevant and needs no acquisition. Nothing in the sweep bears on the catalog coding. As a by-product I fetched sources the previously unreachable open-access Blumenfeld 2004 (BLS 30, DOI 10.3765/bls.v30i1.962), which restates the recessive rule (penult if final syllable heavy, else antepenult; final consonants extrametrical; three-syllable window; HL* pitch melody) and so confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and Kiparsky 2003 as deciding source; it does not supersede Kiparsky.

new_statements.quote: Finite verbs, neuter nouns, exocentric compounds, and some other categories are accented according a generalization termed RECESSIVE ACCENT. Final consonants are extrametrical; CV syllables are light, and all other syllables are heavy. ... (2) a. RECESSIVE ACCENT: Accent the penult if the final syllable is heavy, antepenult otherwise. ... the recessive generalization delimits the accentable window in ANY Greek word: the accent cannot stand to the left of the syllable defined by (2)a. ... (3) a. Final consonants are extrametrical. b. A moraic trochee is constructed at the right edge of the word. c. HL* is associated to the head of the word.

new_statements.reading: First-hand phonological analysis (not a grammar): Ancient Greek accent is a pitch/tonal accent (H tone, HL* melody, acute vs circumflex contrasts on long vowels) whose default position is fixed by the recessive rule — penult if the final syllable is heavy, antepenult otherwise, with final consonants extrametrical — and which caps a right-edge three-syllable window for all words; nouns, adjectives and non-finite verbs may carry lexically unpredictable (oxytone/paroxytone) accent within that window. Blumenfeld adds that the lexical phonology is tone-to-stress (a right-edge moraic trochee attracts the HL* fall) while the phrasal component is stress-to-tone with a phrasal default H inserted phrase-finally (his ex. (7)). This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'tonal' coding and its deciding quotation (Kiparsky 2003's recessive-accent statement is the same generalization, with the same final-syllable weight condition). It was on the audit wishlist as unreachable (403/timeout on 2026-09-12 and 09-16) and is now held.

sources.quote: 'La détermination de la place de l'accent (particulièrement de l'accent récessif, qui n'est que phonologiquement conditionné) en grec ancien fait apparaître clairement la nécessité de disposer de représentations phonologiques où une structure syllabique est définie.' Only p.81 reachable; the HL* analysis itself (relayed by Golston & Paulsen 2023, held) was not read.

sources.note: HL* analysis (H docks before the metrically strong syllable) cited by Golston & Paulsen 2023 as evidence that pitch peak and metrical head dissociate; relevant to the tonal-vs-stress classification. Persée PDF is open but captcha-gated; only p.81 fetched sources.
